notes.30:17: Greek Melchol (also 30:19) is the Septuagint form of the Ammonite deity Malcam/Milcom. In 30:18-20, the Greek reads "her altars" (Hebrew "her daughters/villages"), "his dominion," and "the plains of the Anakim" (Greek Enakeim), and omits MT 49:6 (no verse 30:22).
notes.30:23: Greek aulē ("court," also 30:25, 28) translates the Hebrew place name Hazor as a common noun, Kedem transliterates the Hebrew word for "east," and plēsate ("fill") stands where the Hebrew has "devastate." In 30:27, Greek kekramenous is a metathesized form of kekarmenous ("clipped/shaved"), referring to trimming the hair at the temples.
notes.30:29: Greek Themar is a distinct Septuagint proper name where the Hebrew text reads Hamath, and in 30:33 Greek huiou Hader ("the son of Hader") corresponds to Hebrew Ben-hadad. In 30:31, the Greek reads active "How has she not forsaken My city? They loved a village."
notes.31:1: Jeremiah 31 in the Septuagint corresponds to Jeremiah 48 in the Hebrew Bible. The Greek reads two place names, Hamath and Hagath, where the Hebrew text reads "the fortress [Misgab] and is dismayed."
notes.31:5: The Greek reads the place name Haloth here (and Zoar in v. 4) where the Hebrew text reads "the ascent of Luhith" (and "her little ones" in v. 4).
notes.31:21: The Greek treats Mishor (Hebrew "the tableland/plain") as a place name and reads Rephas and Mophas where the Hebrew text has Jahzah and Mephaath.
notes.31:31: The Greek reads "Kir-hadas of drought" here (and "shorn people" in v. 36) where the Hebrew text has the place name Kir-heres.
notes.31:32: The Greek reads the place name Oserema where the Hebrew text reads Sibmah.
notes.31:33: The Greek pronoun "these" (haide, mirrored by hoide in 32:30) reflects a Greek rendering of the Hebrew vintage shout hedad.
notes.31:34: The Greek reads Etam and "a message of Salasia" where the Hebrew text has Elealeh and Eglath-shelishiyah (or "a three-year-old heifer").
notes.31:41: The Greek reads Ekron here (and omits the eagle imagery of v. 40) where the Hebrew text reads Kerioth.
notes.32:15: Jeremiah 32:15-38 in the Septuagint corresponds to Jeremiah 25:15-38 in the Hebrew Bible. The Greek reads "unmixed wine" (undiluted, full-strength wine) where the Hebrew text reads "wine of wrath."
notes.32:20: Greek allophyloi (lit., "foreigners" or "people of another tribe") is the standard Septuagint designation for the Philistines.
notes.32:23: The Greek reads Teman and Rosh where the Hebrew text reads Tema and Buz.
notes.32:25: The Greek reads "the Persians" here (and "from the east" in v. 26) where the Hebrew text reads "the Medes" (and "from the north" in v. 26).
notes.32:34: The Greek reads "like the choice rams" where the Hebrew text reads "like a choice vessel."
notes.33:1: Greek reads "In the beginning of King Jehoiakim" rather than "the reign of Jehoiakim" (MT 26:1); in the Septuagint chapter arrangement, Jeremiah 33-35 correspond to MT Jeremiah 26-28.
notes.33:2: Greek reads "all the Judeans" where MT 26:2 has "all the cities of Judah." In v. 3 (and vv. 13, 19), Greek translates the Hebrew for God relenting with the verb "cease" (pauomai).
notes.33:7: Here and in vv. 8, 11, 16 (as well as 34:9 and 35:1), the Greek explicitly designates Jeremiah's opponents as "false prophets" (pseudoprophetai), where the Hebrew has "prophets."
notes.33:9: Greek opens with "because" (hoti) rather than the Hebrew question "Why" (MT 26:9), linking the accusation directly to the threat of death in v. 8.
notes.34:2: Greek kloios denotes a wooden or iron neck collar (rendering the Hebrew term for yoke-bars). Verses 1, 7, 13, 17, and 21 are absent from the Septuagint text of this chapter (MT Jer 27).
notes.34:3: Greek reads "Idumea," the Hellenistic name for Edom, and includes the phrase "to meet them," which has no direct equivalent in MT 27:3.
notes.34:5: Greek epicheiron ("arm," also in 31:25) here renders the Hebrew "outstretched arm." In v. 6, the Greek omits the title "My servant" for Nebuchadnezzar (cf. MT 27:6).
notes.34:11: Greek reads masculine "for him" (auto), referring to the king of Babylon, whereas MT 27:11 has feminine "till it," referring to the land.
notes.34:18: Greek reads "let them meet with Me" (apantesatosan moi), continuing the Lord's first-person voice from v. 16 rather than the third-person "entreat the Lord of hosts" in MT 27:18. In v. 15, the Greek pairs "unjustly" (ep' adiko) with "false things" (pseude).
notes.35:1: As in chs. 33-34, the Greek explicitly labels Hananiah "the false prophet" (ho pseudoprophetes), where MT 28:1 reads "the prophet."
notes.35:9: Greek uses the active verb "they will know" with "to them" and renders the Hebrew "in truth" with en pistei ("in faithfulness").
notes.35:13: Greek reads first-person "I will make" (poieso), attributing the iron collars directly to the Lord, whereas MT 28:13 has second-person "you have made."
notes.36:1: The Greek explicitly reads "the false prophets" (MT: "the prophets") and adds "a letter to Babylon for the exiles." Throughout this chapter, LXX ch. 36 corresponds to MT ch. 29, with several substantial differences.
notes.36:11: Instead of the MT's "For I know the plans I have for you ... to give you a future and a hope," the Greek reads "and I will plan for you a plan of peace and not evil things, to give you these things." The Greek also shortens v. 14 and omits vv. 16-20 entirely, connecting v. 15 directly into v. 21.
notes.36:24: The Greek reads "the Elamite" (ton Ailameiten), a distinct gentilic name where the Hebrew MT has "the Nehelamite" (likewise in 36:31).
notes.36:25: In vv. 25-28 the Greek diverges sharply from the MT: instead of reporting that Shemaiah sent letters in his own name, the Lord tells Jeremiah to say to Shemaiah "I did not send you in My name" and then directly commands Jeremiah to address Zephaniah (with v. 27 lacking "not" and v. 28 reading "to you" rather than "to us").
notes.37:6: The Greek includes the difficult clause "and concerning fear in which they will hold loins and deliverance" (absent from MT), reads "because" (dioti) rather than "why," and renders the pallor of the faces literally as "jaundice" (ikteron).
notes.37:12: The Greek reads "I have raised up a fracture" (Anestesa syntrimma), where the Hebrew MT has "Your hurt is incurable." Verses 10-11, 15, and 22 are absent from the Greek text of this chapter (MT ch. 30).
notes.37:16: Instead of the MT's "every one of them shall go into captivity," the Greek reads "all your enemies will eat all their flesh," and includes the clause on multiplied sins (with plural "they did these things to you") within v. 16 rather than v. 15.
notes.37:17: The Greek reads "She is your prey" (thereuma hymon estin), reflecting a different reading of the Hebrew consonants where the MT has "It is Zion."
notes.37:18: The Greek reads "his captivity" (MT: "his dwellings") and "the people" (ho laos; MT: "the palace"), and in v. 20 reads "their testimonies" (MT: "his congregation").
notes.38:1: Jeremiah 38 in the Septuagint corresponds to Jeremiah 31 in the Hebrew Bible (including the New Covenant oracle in 38:31-37).
notes.38:2: The Greek reads 'I found warmth in the wilderness with those who perished by the sword,' a distinctive Septuagint rendering differing from the Masoretic Text ('the people who survived the sword found grace').
notes.38:8: The Greek reads 'at the feast of Passover' (en heorte phasek), a notable Septuagint reading where the Masoretic Text has 'among them the blind and the lame.'
notes.38:21: The Greek reads 'Zion,' 'make retribution,' 'set your heart on the shoulders,' and 'mourning,' reflecting distinctive Septuagint renderings where the Masoretic Text speaks of setting up road markers and signposts toward the highway.
notes.38:35: Verses 35-37 follow a different order from the Masoretic Text (31:37, 35, 36), and verse 35 reads 'then I will not reject the family of Israel,' where the Masoretic Text's apodosis is positive ('I will reject').
notes.38:38: The Greek names 'Hanamel' (Hanameel) where the Masoretic Text reads 'Hananel.'
notes.38:40: The Greek retains two untranslated Hebrew geographical terms as 'Hasaremoth' (hasaremoth, corresponding to the fields/terraces) and 'Nachal Kidron' (nachal Kedron, 'wadi/brook of Kidron').
notes.39:8: The Greek text reads "Samol" (a metathesis of "Shallum" in v. 7) and "you are the elder" (Greek presbyteros), where the Hebrew MT reads "Shallum" and "the right of redemption is yours."
notes.39:15: The Greek reads ktisthesontai ("will be established/founded," from ktizo), contrasting with ktethesontai ("will be bought," from ktaomai) in v. 43; this reflects either an ancient Greek variant or the dual sense of Hebrew qanah ("acquire/create").
notes.39:17: "O Existing One, Lord" renders Greek Ho on Kyrie, echoing the divine title in Exod 3:14 ("the One who is"), while "nothing will be hidden from You" (also v. 27) renders Greek apokrybe where the Hebrew MT has "too difficult."
notes.39:35: "Molech the king" preserves the Greek doublet to Moloch basilei, rendering Hebrew lammolekh both as a proper name and as "king."
notes.39:39: "another way and another heart" faithfully reflects Greek hodon heteran kai kardian heteran, differing in both order and wording ("another" vs. "one") from the Hebrew MT's "one heart and one way."
notes.40:4: "for ramparts and bulwarks" translates Greek eis charakas kai promachonas, whereas the Hebrew MT reads "against the siege mounds and the sword."
notes.40:6: The Greek interposes "and I will heal it" (kai iatreuso auten) between "and I will reveal to them" (kai phaneroso autois) and its object "both peace and faithfulness" (kai eirenen kai pistin), preserving the distinctive clause order of the Septuagint.
notes.40:9: "be embittered" translates Greek pikranthesontai (matching "embitter" in 39:32), where the Hebrew MT has "tremble."
notes.40:13: The Septuagint concludes chapter 40 here (corresponding to MT 33:13), lacking the passage found in MT 33:14-26.
notes.41:1: The Greek literally reads "were fighting against him" before "against Jerusalem," a difficult reading likely arising from rendering a Hebrew phrase meaning "with him" as an object pronoun or anticipating Judah or Zedekiah.
notes.41:5: The Septuagint reads "wept for" and "even to Hades they will mourn for you," differing from the Hebrew text's burning of spices and lament "Alas, lord!"
notes.41:10: The Septuagint moves directly to the people turning back, omitting the initial compliance reported in the Hebrew text. The printed verb form (from eao, "left") can alternatively be accented as an aorist of otheo ("forced" or "drove"), matching the Hebrew sense of subjugating them.
notes.41:18: The Greek reads "the calf that they made to serve it," departing from the Hebrew covenant-cutting ritual ("the calf that they cut in two and passed between its parts").
notes.41:21: The Greek shifts to a nominative noun phrase paired with a dative participle ("and the force of the king of Babylon [is] for those who are running away from them"), whereas the Hebrew coordinates the army under "into the hand of" as those who have withdrawn.
notes.42:2: Greek "Archabin" transliterates the Hebrew definite article and plural name for "the Rechabites" (compare "Rechab" in vv. 6 and 14-19); "courts" likewise follows the Greek text where the Hebrew has "chambers."
notes.42:3: The Greek names Jeconiah, Jeremin, and Chabasin correspond respectively to Jaazaniah, Jeremiah, and Habazziniah in the Hebrew text.
notes.42:4: The Greek expands the genealogy to three generations, "Jonan son of Hananiah, son of Gedaliah," where the Hebrew text has "Hanan son of Igdaliah."
notes.42:11: The Greek reads "the Assyrians," whereas the Hebrew text reads "the Arameans" (Syrians).
notes.42:18: Unlike the Hebrew text, which inserts a transition addressing the house of the Rechabites and repeats the messenger formula in v. 19, the Greek proceeds directly into a single oracle ending with "all the days of the earth" in v. 19.
notes.43:7: The Greek literally reads "their mercy" (ἔλεος), an LXX rendering of the Hebrew word for "supplication" or "plea for mercy" (compare 44:20).
notes.43:9: The Septuagint dates the fast to "the eighth year" of Jehoiakim, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew text (Jer 36:9) reads "the fifth year."
notes.43:12: The Septuagint names "Jonathan" (Ἰωναθάν) son of Achbor here rather than Elnathan as in the Hebrew text, though Elnathan appears in v. 25.
notes.43:20: Here and in v. 21 the Septuagint reads the shorter name "Elisha" (Ἐλεισά) rather than "Elishama" (Ἐλεισαμά) as in v. 12.
notes.43:25: Unlike the Hebrew text, where Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah urge the king not to burn the scroll, the Septuagint names only Elnathan and Gedaliah (Γοδολίας) and states that they advised the king to burn it.
notes.44:5: The Greek literally reads "went up against Jerusalem" (ἐπὶ Ἰερουσαλήμ), differing from the Hebrew text (Jer 37:5) and v. 11 below, where the Chaldeans withdraw "from Jerusalem."
notes.44:12: The Greek reads "to buy from there" (τοῦ ἀγοράσαι ἐκεῖθεν), rendering a difficult Hebrew verb often understood as taking possession of a portion of property.
notes.44:13: The Septuagint describes the official as "a man with whom he was lodging" (rather than a captain of the guard) and names him "Saruiah" (Σαρουιά, here and in v. 14) instead of the Hebrew "Irijah."
notes.44:16: The word "chereth" (χερέθ) is an untranslated Greek transliteration corresponding to the Hebrew term for vaulted cells or chambers.
notes.44:20: As in 43:7, "my mercy" (τὸ ἔλεός μου) reflects the Hebrew idiom for a plea for mercy; the Septuagint also frames the second half of the verse as a question ("why are you returning me ... and will I not die there?") rather than a negative petition.
notes.45:1: The Greek names Saphanias son of Nathan (corresponding to Hebrew Shephatiah son of Mattan) and lists three officials rather than four (omitting Pashhur son of Malchijah).
notes.45:2: Greek heurema literally means "a find" or "unexpected gain," rendering the Hebrew idiom for escaping with one's life as a prize of war (so also in 46:18).
notes.45:4: Greek chresimologei is a rare verb meaning "speaks beneficially" or a variant of chresmologei ("prophesies/delivers oracles"), where the Hebrew text reads "seeks."
notes.45:9: The Greek has Ebed-melech accuse the king directly ("You have acted wickedly in what you have done"), whereas the Hebrew text directs the charge against the officials ("these men").
notes.45:14: Haseleisel (Greek haseleisel) is an untranslated Septuagint transliteration corresponding to the Hebrew "the third [entrance]."
notes.46:1: The Greek reads "in the ninth month of Zedekiah," whereas the Hebrew text reads "in the ninth year of Zedekiah... in the tenth month."
notes.46:3: Marganasar, Samagoth, Nabusachar, Nabusaris, Nagargasnaser, and Rabamath are the Septuagint's distinct transliterations of the Babylonian officials' names and titles, differing in form from the Hebrew text.
notes.46:14: In the Septuagint, the narrative passes directly from verse 3 to verse 14, omitting the account of Zedekiah's flight, capture, and blinding found in Hebrew Jeremiah 39:4-13.
notes.47:1: Greek archimageiros ("chief cook") is the Septuagint's literal rendering of the Hebrew title for the captain of the imperial guard. The Greek also reads "from Daman" where the Hebrew text has "from Ramah."
notes.47:8: The Greek names Jophe (corresponding to Hebrew Ephai) and lists only Johanan son of Kareah (omitting Jonathan).
notes.47:9: The Greek reads "the servants of the Chaldeans," reflecting a different reading of the Hebrew consonants that the Masoretic Text vocalizes as "serving the Chaldeans."
notes.47:14: Belisa is the Septuagint's form of the Ammonite king's name, corresponding to Hebrew Baalis.
notes.48:1: The Greek reads Elasa, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has Elishama.
notes.48:5: The Greek names Salem (where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads Shiloh) and uses the Greek word manna to represent the Hebrew grain offering (minchah).
notes.48:6: In the Greek text the visiting men are the ones walking along and weeping, whereas the Hebrew text describes Ishmael as weeping as he went out.
notes.48:9: The Greek reads "this is a great cistern," reflecting a well-known textual variant compared with the Hebrew text's "by the side of Gedaliah."
notes.48:10: The Greek "turned back" differs from the Hebrew "took captive," and "chief cook" (Greek archimageiros) is the standard Septuagint rendering of the Babylonian official title "captain of the guard."
notes.48:17: Gaberochamaa is the Greek transliteration of the place name rendered Geruth Chimham in the Hebrew text; similarly, "the rest" in 48:16 and 50:6 translates Greek ta loipa where the Hebrew has "the little ones."
notes.49:1: The Greek reads Azariah son of Maaseiah here (as in 50:2), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah.
notes.49:10: Greek anapepaumai literally means "I have rested" or "I have ceased," here rendering the Hebrew verb for "relent."
notes.49:12: All three verbs in the Greek are first person ("I will give... I will have mercy... and return"), making the Lord the subject of each action, whereas in the Hebrew text the last two refer to the king of Babylon.
notes.49:17: The phrase "and all the foreigners" is distinctive to the Greek text and does not appear in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.50:2: The Greek reads Maaseiah (where the Hebrew text has Hoshaiah) and "all the men who addressed Jeremiah" (where the Hebrew text has "all the arrogant men").
notes.50:9: Greek en prothyrois ("in the entranceway") differs from the Hebrew text's "in the mortar in the brick terrace."
notes.50:10: The Greek reads "that you hid" (second person, addressing Jeremiah) and "he will lift up weapons against them," whereas the Hebrew text reads "that I have hidden" and "he will spread his canopy over them."
notes.50:12: Greek phtheirizo literally means "delouse" (pick lice off), a well-known Septuagint rendering where the Hebrew text reads "wrap himself in."
notes.50:13: The Greek identifies the site as Heliopolis (the city of the Sun) in On, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Beth-shemesh in the land of Egypt."
notes.51:6: Greek reads "in the gates of Judah and outside Jerusalem" (similarly "outside Jerusalem" in 51:9, 17, 21), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem."
notes.51:21: The Greek text reads the first-person plural "that we burned" (ethumiasamen), shifting immediately to "you and your fathers"; the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads second-person plural throughout.
notes.51:27: Greek reads ean ekliposin ("if they come to an end"); the phrase is often taken as equivalent to heos an ekliposin ("until they come to an end"), the sense of the Hebrew text.
notes.51:33: Greek reads "I lay down in groanings" (ekoimethen, "lay down/slept"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "I am weary with my groaning."
notes.52:4: Verses 52:2-3 of the Hebrew numbering are absent from the Septuagint. Greek reads "in the ninth month" (Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "tenth month"); "four-footed siegeworks" renders Greek tetrapodois, understood either as wooden siege barricades or (as a spelling of tetrapedois) four-foot stone blocks.
notes.52:9: Greek Deblatha (also in 52:10, 26, 27) corresponds to Hebrew Riblah, reflecting a common daleth/resh consonant variation.
notes.52:12: Greek archimageiros ("chief cook," also in 52:14, 16, 19, 24, 26) is the Septuagint's literal rendering of the Hebrew royal-military title rab-tabbachim ("captain of the guard" or "chief of the slaughterers").
notes.52:19: Greek sapphoth and masmaroth are untranslated transliterations of Hebrew temple vessel terms (likely "basins" and "wick trimmers/snuffers").
notes.52:21: Greek reads "thirty-five cubits" (matching 2 Chronicles 3:15; Hebrew Jeremiah 52:21 reads "eighteen cubits"); in 52:22, Greek also uniquely adds "eight pomegranates to the cubit for the twelve cubits."
notes.52:31: Verses 52:28-30 of the Hebrew numbering (the exile deportation totals) are absent from the Septuagint. Greek reads "Jehoiakim" (Ioakeim, the form the Septuagint regularly uses for both Jehoiakim and Jehoiachin), "twenty-fourth" (Hebrew "twenty-fifth"), transcribes Evil-merodach as Oulaimadachar, and uniquely adds "and cut his hair" (kai ekeiren auton) after "lifted up" (literally "took") his head.

unplaced.text: At the beginning of the reign of King Zedekiah, this word came concerning Elam.
unplaced.note: In the Saints Greek Critical Text this dating notice closes the oracle against Elam; it has no separate place in the Saints.Bible numbering, so it is shown after 25:19.
